facts.Acorn Woodpecker: These woodpeckers drill thousands of holes into a single granary tree, wedging one acorn into each to stockpile food for winter.
facts.Alpine Swift: The alpine swift is one of the most aerial of all birds, and tracked individuals have stayed airborne for over six months without ever landing, feeding, sleeping, and even mating on the wing. It is among the fastest birds in level flight, clocked at over 100 miles per hour in courtship chases. Nesting in cliffs and tall buildings across southern Europe, Asia, and Africa, it forms long-lived pairs that return to the same crevice year after year. Its short legs and long scimitar wings make it almost helpless on the ground, so it virtually never perches.
facts.American Coot: Despite swimming like ducks, coots have lobed rather than webbed toes, and they detect and reject parasitic eggs laid in their nests.
facts.American Flamingo: The American Flamingo's vivid pink comes entirely from carotenoid pigments in the algae and brine shrimp it filters from briny lagoons; a poor diet fades captive birds to pale white. It feeds with its head upside down underwater, the bill working like a sieve to strain tiny organisms from mud and water. Parents of both sexes produce a bright red crop milk to feed chicks, and the secretion's pigment can temporarily drain the adults' own color. Highly social, flamingos nest in dense colonies on cone-shaped mud mounds and perform synchronized group displays of head-flagging and wing-saluting.
facts.American Goldfinch: The American Goldfinch is a strict vegetarian, feeding almost exclusively on seeds, and times its breeding unusually late, often into July and August, to coincide with the peak of thistle and other seed sources. This diet is a lethal trap for parasitic Brown-headed Cowbirds, whose chicks cannot survive on the all-seed regurgitation goldfinches feed their young. The males molt twice a year, trading their brilliant lemon-yellow summer plumage for drab olive in winter. In flight they bound through the air in deep undulating arcs, often calling a cheerful per-chick-o-ree at the top of each rise.
facts.American Kestrel: The American Kestrel is North America's smallest and most colorful falcon, barely the size of a mourning dove yet a fierce predator of insects, voles, and small birds. It can perceive ultraviolet light, allowing it to track the UV-reflective urine trails that rodents leave across grassland, and it hovers on rapidly beating wings while scanning for prey. Kestrels nest in tree cavities and nest boxes, and they characteristically bob their tails and heads while perched on wires.
facts.Aplomado Falcon: The aplomado falcon is a slender, long-tailed raptor of open grasslands from the American Southwest down into South America. Pairs are renowned for cooperative hunting: one falcon flushes prey such as birds or large insects from cover while its mate waits in ambush to seize the fleeing quarry in midair. Long-legged for a falcon, it will also pursue prey on foot through grass and even chase animals flushed by grass fires. Once nearly gone from the United States, it has been the focus of intensive reintroduction efforts in Texas and New Mexico.
facts.Arctic Tern: The Arctic Tern makes the longest migration of any animal, tracing a zigzagging route of up to 90,000 kilometers a year between Arctic breeding grounds and the Antarctic pack ice. Because it chases endless summer at both ends of the planet, it sees more daylight in a year than any other creature, and over a lifespan of thirty years may travel a distance equal to three round trips to the Moon. A graceful, deeply forked-tailed seabird, it plunge-dives for small fish and crustaceans and defends its colony fiercely, dive-bombing intruders and drawing blood with its sharp red bill.
facts.Bar-tailed Godwit: The Bar-tailed Godwit holds the record for the longest known nonstop flight of any bird: one satellite-tagged individual flew over 13,000 kilometers from Alaska to Tasmania in eleven days without once landing to eat, drink, or rest. To prepare, godwits nearly double their body weight in fat and shrink their digestive organs to lighten the load, essentially flying as a fueled wing. They navigate vast open ocean with no landmarks, riding favorable weather systems southward across the Pacific. These long-billed shorebirds probe tidal mudflats for worms and clams, and gather in huge flocks at staging grounds before each leg of the journey.
facts.Barn Owl: The barn owl is the most widely distributed owl on Earth, found on every continent except Antarctica, and a peerless nocturnal hunter. Its facial disc funnels sound to ears set at slightly different heights, letting it pinpoint prey in total darkness by sound alone and strike a scurrying mouse with deadly precision. Specialized comb-like fringes on its flight feathers muffle turbulence, granting near-silent flight. A single family can consume thousands of rodents a year, making the barn owl a prized natural pest controller. Its eerie, rasping shriek is unlike the hoot of other owls.
facts.Barn Swallow: The Barn Swallow is the most widespread swallow on Earth, breeding across the Northern Hemisphere and wintering as far as southern Africa and South America, absent only from Antarctica. It builds an open cup nest from hundreds of mud pellets mixed with grass, almost always on human structures like barns, bridges, and culverts. An aerial insectivore, it feeds entirely on the wing, swooping low over fields and water to snatch flies and other insects, often drinking and bathing in mid-flight. Its deeply forked tail and long outer streamers aid the sharp, acrobatic turns that hunting demands.
facts.Baya Weaver: The baya weaver is a sparrow-sized South Asian songbird renowned as a master architect among birds. Breeding males weave intricate retort-shaped nests with long downward entrance tunnels, knotting and looping strips of grass and palm leaf into a hanging flask that sways from a branch over water. A male may build several partial nests, and females inspect the craftsmanship before choosing a mate and the structure they prefer. Folklore and some observers report the birds embedding mud, and even fireflies, inside the nest. Colonies of dozens of these woven baskets festoon a single tree.
facts.Belted Kingfisher: The Belted Kingfisher excavates a nesting burrow up to eight feet long into a vertical riverbank, both parents digging with their bills and shoving soil out with their feet. It is one of the few bird species in which the female is more colorful than the male, wearing a rust-colored band across the breast that he lacks. Perching above clear water or hovering on rattling wingbeats, it plunges headfirst to seize fish, then beats them against a branch before swallowing them head-down. Indigestible bones and scales are later coughed up as compact pellets.
facts.Black Skimmer: The Black Skimmer is a striking coastal bird with a knife-thin, uniquely structured bill whose lower mandible is markedly longer than the upper. It feeds by flying low and fast with that elongated lower bill slicing the water's surface, snapping the bill shut the instant it touches a fish. Skimmers are among the few birds with vertical, cat-like pupils that can close to a narrow slit, shielding their eyes from the glare of sun on sand and water. They nest in dense colonies on open beaches.
facts.Black-Necked Stilt: Relative to body size the Black-necked Stilt has among the longest legs of any bird, second only to flamingos, wading on slender pink stilts through shallow wetlands and salt ponds. It feeds with delicate sideways sweeps of its needle-thin bill, snatching aquatic insects, tiny crustaceans, and brine flies from the water's surface. Highly vocal and territorial, nesting colonies erupt in piercing yapping alarm calls and will mob intruding hawks or coyotes en masse. Chicks leave the simple ground scrape within a day of hatching and can wade and feed themselves almost immediately.
facts.Black-billed Magpie: The black-billed magpie is a strikingly long-tailed corvid of western North America with iridescent green-blue wings and a reputation for sharp intelligence. Magpies are among the few non-mammals to pass the mirror self-recognition test, touching a coloured mark on their own bodies seen only in reflection. They famously gather in noisy congregations around dead members of their kind, behavior likened to funerals. Resourceful omnivores, they cache surplus food, follow large mammals to pick ticks and carrion, and build elaborate domed nests with a roof of sticks.
facts.Blue Jay: Blue Jays are bold, vocal corvids known for mimicking the screams of hawks, a trick that can clear feeders of competitors or warn flockmates of real danger. Their blue coloration is not pigment but structural color, produced when light scatters off microscopic features in the feathers; crush the feather and the blue vanishes. Each autumn jays cache thousands of acorns, and the ones they forget help plant new oak forests. Highly intelligent, they form long-term pair bonds and travel in loose, loud family groups.
facts.Carolina Wren: Only the male sings, belting a loud "teakettle-teakettle" up to thousands of times a day despite weighing barely 20 grams.
facts.Cedar Waxwing: It can get drunk and even die from eating overripe, fermented berries, and pairs pass food back and forth during courtship.
facts.Clark's Nutcracker: Clark's nutcracker is a pale grey corvid of high western mountains, famous as one of nature's greatest food hoarders. Each autumn a single bird harvests pine seeds in a special throat pouch and buries them in tens of thousands of small caches, sometimes up to 30,000 seeds across many square kilometers. Months later, even under snow, it relocates the bulk of these stores from memory with extraordinary spatial recall, and the seeds it forgets grow into new pines. This tight partnership makes the nutcracker the chief planter of whitebark and limber pine forests.
facts.Cliff Swallow: Hundreds of pairs build gourd-shaped mud nests in dense colonies, and they famously return to Mission San Juan Capistrano.
facts.Common Nightjar: The Common Nightjar, or Eurasian Nightjar, is a nocturnal insect-hunter so superbly camouflaged in mottled grey and brown that it nearly vanishes against bark or leaf litter while roosting motionless by day. At dusk males deliver a long, mechanical churring song that can continue for minutes, and they slap their wings together in moth-hunting display flights. Their wide gaping mouths, fringed with sensitive bristles, scoop moths and beetles from the air on the wing. An old folk name, goatsucker, arose from the myth that the birds drank milk from livestock they were actually hunting insects around.
facts.Common Raven: The Common Raven ranks among the most intelligent of all birds, solving multi-step puzzles, fashioning and using tools, and demonstrating the ability to plan for future events, performance that rivals great apes in some laboratory tests. Ravens recognize individual human faces, hold grudges, and engage in playful aerial acrobatics including barrel rolls and carrying objects in flight to drop and catch. They cache surplus food and will pretend to hide it when watched, an apparent grasp of deception. Mated pairs are lifelong, defending large territories with a remarkable vocabulary of croaks, knocks, and mimicked sounds.
facts.Cooper's Hawk: Cooper's hawk is a medium-sized woodland accipiter built for explosive agility, with short rounded wings and a long rudder-like tail that lets it weave through dense branches at speed in pursuit of songbirds and doves. The chase is so violent that studies of skeletons have found a large fraction of birds carry healed fractures in the chest and wishbone from collisions with branches and prey. It kills by squeezing prey in its talons rather than biting, sometimes drowning a victim. Once a shy forest bird, it has become a common and bold hunter at suburban feeders.
facts.Crested Caracara: The crested caracara is an unusual member of the falcon family that behaves more like a vulture and a ground-bird than a high-flying raptor. It often hunts and forages on foot, striding boldly across open country to snatch reptiles, insects, small mammals, and carrion, and will harass true vultures to rob them of carcasses. Bold and conspicuous with its black cap, bare orange face, and pale neck, it ranges from the southern United States through much of South America. It is the national bird of Mexico and features in Aztec iconography.
facts.Dalmatian Pelican: The Dalmatian pelican is among the heaviest flying birds in the world, with a wingspan that can exceed three metres. In the breeding season the drab grey-white adult transforms, its throat pouch flushing a fiery orange-red and a curled mane of feathers rising on its nape. It fishes cooperatively, with groups sometimes herding fish into the shallows before scooping them up in their vast pouches. Once severely threatened by wetland drainage and persecution, careful conservation around lakes in Greece and the Balkans has helped its numbers recover.
facts.European Starling: The European Starling's North American population descends from roughly a hundred birds released in 1890s New York, and now numbers in the hundreds of millions across the continent. A gifted vocal mimic, the starling weaves imitations of other birds, car alarms, and mechanical sounds into its rambling songs. In autumn and winter huge flocks gather into murmurations, swirling shapes of thousands of birds that twist in unison to confuse predators like falcons. Starlings also seasonally change appearance as their winter white-spotted plumage wears away to reveal glossy iridescent breeding feathers.
facts.Fork-tailed Drongo: The fork-tailed drongo of sub-Saharan Africa is a glossy black, deeply forked-tailed bird with a brilliant talent for deception. It often follows meerkats and other foragers, giving honest alarm calls when real predators appear, which earns it trust. But it also mimics the alarm calls of those same animals and of other birds when no danger exists, sending them fleeing so it can swoop in and steal the food they abandon. Studies show it varies its false calls to avoid being ignored, a rare example of tactical deception in animals.
facts.Golden Bowerbird: The golden bowerbird is the smallest of all bowerbirds, a compact olive-and-gold songbird of the cool upland rainforests of northeastern Queensland. The male is an extraordinary builder, raising a 'maypole' bower of two tall stick towers, sometimes nearly three meters high, joined by a display perch and adorned with pale lichen, flowers, and fruit. These towers are among the largest structures built by any songbird relative to its size, and a successful male may maintain the same bower for years. The species feeds mainly on fruit and is restricted to a few mist-shrouded mountaintops.
facts.Golden Eagle: The golden eagle is one of the most powerful raptors in the Northern Hemisphere, with a wingspan exceeding two meters and a hunting stoop that can surpass 240 kilometers per hour, ending in a strike from talons that exert bone-crushing force. Fiercely territorial, a single pair may patrol dozens of square kilometers and reuse massive cliff or tree eyries for generations, adding sticks each year. It takes hares, marmots, and even young deer, and trained golden eagles have hunted alongside Central Asian falconers for centuries. Revered across many cultures, it appears on numerous national emblems.
facts.Great Blue Heron: The Great Blue Heron is North America's largest heron, standing over a meter tall with a wingspan approaching two meters, yet weighing only a few kilograms thanks to hollow bones. It hunts by standing utterly motionless in shallow water before spearing or seizing fish, frogs, and even small mammals with a lightning strike of its dagger bill. Specialized 'powder down' feathers on its chest continually fray into a fine powder the bird uses to clean fish slime and oils from its plumage. Herons nest colonially in tall trees, returning to the same rookeries year after year.
facts.Greater Bird-of-Paradise: Male Greater Birds-of-Paradise gather in traditional treetop arenas called leks, where they raise cascades of golden-yellow flank plumes and strike rigid poses to dazzle visiting females. The species is the largest in its genus, and only mature males develop the full ornamental plumage, which takes years to acquire. Native to lowland forests of New Guinea and the Aru Islands, they feed mainly on fruit and some insects, helping disperse rainforest seeds. The lavish plumes once drove a devastating feather trade before protections curbed the hunting.
facts.Green Heron: The Green Heron is a small, stocky, solitary wader that hunts at the water's edge with extraordinary patience, often crouched motionless for long stretches. It is one of the very few birds known to use tools as bait: it drops insects, feathers, twigs, or even bits of bread onto the water's surface to lure curious fish within striking range. Compact and dark, it crooks its neck low while stalking, then unfurls it in a lightning thrust to seize prey.
facts.Green Jay: The Green Jay is a vivid tropical corvid of brushlands from south Texas through Central and South America, splashed in lime green, blue, and black with a striking facial mask. In the Texas population, these clever jays have been observed using twigs as tools to pry up loose bark and flush out hidden insects, a rare feat of avian tool use. They live in tight family groups in which yearlings help defend the territory, and their varied repertoire includes a remarkable imitation of hawk calls.
facts.House Sparrow: The House Sparrow is among the most widespread wild birds on Earth, having spread alongside human settlements to every continent except Antarctica. Tightly tied to people, it nests in building cavities, signs, and streetlights, and rarely strays far from human activity. Highly social, sparrows feed and dust-bathe in noisy flocks and establish dominance through the size of the black throat 'badge' males wear. Despite their abundance, populations have declined sharply in many cities, making them an unexpected barometer of urban health.
facts.Kea: The kea is the world's only true alpine parrot, an olive-green bird with flame-orange underwings that thrives in the snowfields and beech forests of New Zealand's South Island. Famously intelligent and mischievous, keas solve multi-step puzzles, cooperate to obtain food, and even use tools in captivity, and tests suggest they can reason about probability. Their relentless curiosity drives them to shred the rubber seals and windscreen wipers off parked cars and tents. Once persecuted as sheep-killers, they are now a protected and endangered species numbering only a few thousand.
facts.Killdeer: To lure predators from its nest, the killdeer fakes a broken wing, dragging it pitifully along the ground before flying off once the threat follows.
facts.Lilac-breasted Roller: The Lilac-breasted Roller is named for the spectacular aerial 'rolling' courtship of the male, who climbs high then plunges in twisting, side-rolling dives while calling raucously. A sit-and-wait predator of African savannas, it perches conspicuously on bare branches and wires, dropping onto insects, scorpions, lizards, and small rodents below. Its plumage layers lilac, turquoise, and green, with bright blue flight feathers flashing in flight. Pairs are strongly territorial and will mob raptors far larger than themselves.
facts.Loggerhead Shrike: The Loggerhead Shrike, nicknamed the 'butcher bird,' impales prey such as insects, lizards, small rodents, and even other birds on thorns, barbed wire, and sharp twigs. This larder lets it store surplus food and helps it handle toxic prey like lubber grasshoppers, which become edible after a few days of weathering. Lacking the powerful talons of true raptors, the shrike uses its hooked, notched bill to deliver a precise killing bite to the neck. It is a songbird that has evolved a predatory lifestyle, and its populations have declined steeply across North America.
facts.Long-tailed Tit: Long-tailed tits build elaborate elastic nests of moss, spider silk, and up to 6,000 feathers, woven to expand as chicks grow.
facts.Magnificent Frigatebird: The magnificent frigatebird is a vast-winged seabird with the largest wing-area-to-body-weight ratio of any bird, letting it soar for days or even weeks without landing. Breeding males inflate a brilliant scarlet gular pouch into a taut balloon to display for females. Lacking waterproof plumage, frigatebirds never settle on the sea; instead they snatch flying fish from the surface and famously harass other seabirds in mid-air, forcing them to disgorge their catch. They ride storm fronts and trade winds, exploiting rising air to stay aloft with almost no wingbeats.
facts.Malachite Sunbird: Breeding male Malachite Sunbirds gleam with iridescent metallic-green plumage and grow elongated central tail feathers, while females and non-breeding males are a duller olive. They feed largely on nectar, hovering briefly or perching to probe tubular flowers with long, downcurved bills and brush-tipped tongues, and they supplement this with small insects and spiders. Found in highland and fynbos habitats of eastern and southern Africa, they are important pollinators of proteas and aloes. Males fiercely defend nectar-rich territories, chasing off rivals and other nectar-feeders.
facts.Mallard: The mallard is the ancestor of nearly all domestic duck breeds and one of the most widespread waterfowl on the planet, found across the Northern Hemisphere. Counterintuitively it is the female that makes the loud, familiar quacking, while the green-headed male produces only a quieter, raspier call. Mallards readily hybridize with many related duck species, sometimes threatening rarer relatives through genetic swamping. Highly adaptable, they thrive in city parks and farmland as easily as in remote wetlands, and ducklings can swim and feed themselves within hours of hatching.
facts.Malleefowl: The malleefowl is a ground-dwelling Australian megapode that incubates its eggs not with body heat but inside an enormous mound of sand and rotting vegetation, a natural compost incubator. The male labors nearly year-round, raking together a mound that can be meters across, and tests its internal temperature by probing it with his bill, then adding or removing sand to hold it near a steady 33 degrees Celsius. Chicks hatch deep within and dig themselves out fully feathered and able to fly within hours, receiving no parental care. Habitat loss and predators have made the species nationally Vulnerable.
facts.Mandarin Duck: The male mandarin duck is one of the most ornately patterned waterfowl in the world, with orange 'sail' feathers raised like fans on its back, a russet whiskered face, and a purple breast. Native to East Asia, it nests in tree cavities high above ground, and the day-old ducklings make a daring leap from the hole, bouncing unharmed on the forest floor to follow their mother to water. Long a symbol of fidelity in Chinese and Japanese art, mandarin pairs are often depicted together though they do not truly mate for life. Feral populations now thrive in Britain after escaping from captive collections.
facts.Montezuma Oropendola: The Montezuma oropendola is a large, crow-sized blackbird of Central American lowlands, the male glossy chestnut and black with a bright blue cheek patch, bare pink wattle, and pale ivory bill. Its courtship is unforgettable: a male bows forward and tips almost completely upside down on the branch while pouring out a liquid, gurgling, electronic-sounding song. Colonies hang dozens of long woven basket nests from isolated trees, often near wasp nests for protection. Females do all the building and rearing, while a single dominant male fathers most of the colony's young.
facts.Mute Swan: The mute swan is a heavy, elegant waterbird introduced widely beyond its Eurasian range, and despite its name it is far from silent, hissing, grunting, and producing a throbbing musical hum from its wings audible across a quiet lake in flight. It is one of the heaviest flying birds, and a cob defending its nest can break a person's arm with a wing blow. Pairs often mate for life and build huge mounded nests at the water's edge, with both parents shepherding the grey cygnets, sometimes carrying them on their backs. It feeds by upending to graze submerged vegetation.
facts.Northern Gannet: The northern gannet is the largest seabird in the North Atlantic, with a wingspan approaching two metres and a dramatic plunge-diving hunt. It folds its wings and drops from heights of up to 30 metres, hitting the water at around 100 kilometres per hour; air sacs beneath the skin of its face and chest cushion the bone-jarring impact. Gannets nest in dense, clamorous colonies on sea cliffs and islands, some holding tens of thousands of pairs. They have no external nostrils, breathing instead through slits beside the bill to keep water out during dives.
facts.Northern Mockingbird: The Northern Mockingbird is a relentless vocal mimic, and a single male can master over two hundred distinct songs in a lifetime, weaving in the calls of other birds, insects, frogs, and even car alarms and squeaky gates. It often sings through the night, especially unmated males under bright spring moons, repeating each phrase several times before switching. Fiercely territorial, mockingbirds will dive-bomb cats, hawks, and people who stray too near a nest.
facts.Peregrine Falcon: The peregrine falcon is the fastest animal on the planet, exceeding 320 kilometers per hour in a hunting stoop, a vertical plunge in which it strikes flying prey with clenched talons. Bony tubercles in its nostrils baffle the rushing air so it can breathe at speed, and a translucent third eyelid shields its eyes mid-dive. Found on every continent except Antarctica, it has adapted superbly to cities, nesting on skyscraper ledges and bridges and feasting on pigeons. Once devastated by DDT, peregrine populations rebounded dramatically after the pesticide was banned, a landmark conservation success.
facts.Pied Butcherbird: The pied butcherbird is a boldly black-and-white Australian songbird with one of the most celebrated voices in the avian world. Its rich, flute-like phrases are so musically structured, full of clear pitches and varied motifs, that composers have transcribed and performed them as the basis for human music. Males often sing through the night, and birds in a region share and elaborate local song dialects. True to the butcherbird name, it wedges captured insects, lizards, and small birds into forks and barbed wire to hold them while feeding.
facts.Piping Plover: The Piping Plover is a small, pale, sand-colored shorebird that nests in shallow scrapes on open beaches and river sandbars, where its eggs and chicks blend almost invisibly into the substrate. When a predator nears the nest, the adult performs a dramatic broken-wing display, dragging a wing along the sand and feigning injury to lure the threat away before flying off unharmed. Threatened by coastal development and disturbance, it is the focus of intensive beach-protection efforts across its range.
facts.Prairie Falcon: The prairie falcon is a sandy-brown raptor of the arid American West, built for fast, low pursuit over open desert and grassland rather than the high stoop of its peregrine cousin. It hunts ground squirrels and small birds by hugging the terrain at speed and flushing prey, sometimes carrying loads heavier than its own body back to a cliff-ledge scrape. Well adapted to heat, it dumps excess warmth through its bare legs and can range over enormous home territories. Pairs nest on sheer cliff faces, often reusing old raven or eagle ledges.
facts.Purple Martin: The purple martin is North America's largest swallow, an aerial insectivore that catches dragonflies, beetles, and other prey entirely on the wing. East of the Rockies the species is now almost wholly dependent on human-supplied housing, nesting in clustered gourds and multi-room martin houses rather than natural cavities. They are highly colonial and social, returning each spring to the same sites where older 'scout' birds arrive first. Males show a glossy blue-black plumage all over, while females and young are paler and grayer below.
facts.Rainbow Bee-eater: The rainbow bee-eater of Australia is a true insect specialist, taking bees, wasps, and dragonflies on the wing. Before swallowing a stinging insect it returns to a perch and rubs the prey vigorously against the branch to expel the venom and break off the sting. Pairs and helpers excavate long nesting burrows, up to a metre deep, in sandy banks or flat ground. Remarkably tough to digestion, the birds regurgitate the indigestible chitin of their prey as neat pellets.
facts.Red Junglefowl: The Red Junglefowl is the wild ancestor of every domestic chicken on Earth, first domesticated in Southeast Asia thousands of years ago and now spread worldwide through its descendants. A shy forest bird of South and Southeast Asia, the male is far more spectacular than barnyard roosters, wearing glossy golden hackles, a dark iridescent tail, and a bright red comb and wattles that fade during an annual eclipse molt. At dawn males crow loudly to advertise territory, and the species scratches the leaf litter for seeds, insects, and fallen fruit. Genuinely wild birds remain wary and quick to flush into dense cover.
facts.Red-Headed Woodpecker: The Red-headed Woodpecker is one of only a handful of woodpeckers that actively stores food, wedging acorns, beechnuts, and live insects into bark crevices and even sealing the cache in with chips of wood and bark. A striking tricolor bird of black, white, and crimson, it is an unusually skilled flycatcher, hawking insects in midair like a flycatcher rather than only drilling for them. Fiercely territorial, it will destroy the eggs and nests of competitors and raid other birds' stores. Once abundant, the species has declined sharply with the loss of dead standing trees it needs for nesting.
facts.Red-billed Quelea: The red-billed quelea is the most abundant wild bird on Earth, with a post-breeding population estimated at well over a billion. Across sub-Saharan Africa its flocks gather in such density that they wheel through the sky like rolling smoke and can strip a grain field bare in hours, making the species a serious agricultural pest. They breed in immense colonies, sometimes millions of nests packed into a single stretch of thorn scrub. Within a wheeling flock each bird tracks only its nearest neighbors, yet the whole mass turns as one body.
facts.Red-whiskered Bulbul: The Red-whiskered Bulbul, native to South and Southeast Asia, sports a jaunty pointed black crest and a small crimson 'whisker' patch below each eye. Long popular as a cage bird for its lively, cheerful song, escapees and releases have established feral populations far afield, from Florida and Hawaii to Australia and Mauritius. It is an adaptable, gregarious feeder, taking fruit, nectar, and insects, and readily thrives in gardens and urban parks. Noisy and conspicuous, bulbuls move in active chattering groups and can become minor agricultural pests where introduced.
facts.Red-winged Blackbird: A single dominant male defends a marsh territory shared by up to fifteen females, flashing his scarlet shoulder patches to warn off rivals.
facts.Regent Bowerbird: The regent bowerbird is a stunning black-and-gold songbird of eastern Australian rainforests, the male blazing yellow-and-black while females wear muted grey-brown. To win a mate the male builds an avenue bower of twigs and famously paints its inner walls with a homemade greenish 'saliva paint' of chewed plant matter, sometimes wielding a wad of bark as a crude brush, one of the few known examples of tool use in bowerbirds. He decorates the display ground with berries, shells, and other found treasures. The species feeds largely on fruit and helps disperse rainforest seeds.
facts.Rock Pigeon: Rock Pigeons descend from wild cliff-dwelling doves, which is why ledges, bridges, and building cornices serve as perfect substitute nesting sites in cities worldwide. They navigate using the sun, landmarks, smell, and an ability to detect Earth's magnetic field, feats that made them legendary message-carriers for thousands of years. Remarkably, pigeons can recognize themselves in mirrors and distinguish individual human faces and even paintings by different artists. Pairs mate for life, and both parents feed chicks a protein-rich 'crop milk' secreted from the lining of their throats.
facts.Roseate Spoonbill: The Roseate Spoonbill owes its vivid pink to carotenoid pigments absorbed from the crustaceans it eats, so its diet quite literally colors its feathers, deepening to crimson on the shoulders in breeding adults. It feeds by sweeping its flattened, spatula-shaped bill side to side through shallow water, snapping shut on shrimp, small fish, and insects it detects by touch. Highly social, spoonbills feed and nest in noisy mixed colonies with herons, egrets, and ibises. Once nearly wiped out by the plume trade, they have recovered across the Gulf and South American coasts.
facts.Rosy-faced Lovebird: The rosy-faced lovebird is a small, vividly green African parrot with a peach-pink face, named for the intense pair bonds it forms, with mates spending hours preening, feeding, and sitting pressed together. Females show a remarkable nest-building trick, tucking strips of bark and leaves into their rump feathers to ferry several pieces back to the cavity at once. Highly social, they roost and forage in noisy flocks in arid southwestern Africa, and a feral population now thrives in the suburbs of Phoenix, Arizona. Despite the romantic name, a lone lovebird is a stressed one.
facts.Rufous Hummingbird: The Rufous Hummingbird is a pugnacious copper-toned jewel that defends flower patches with relentless aggression, chasing off rivals and even much larger birds. Relative to its body size it undertakes one of the longest migrations of any bird, looping up to 3,900 miles between breeding grounds in Alaska and the Pacific Northwest and wintering sites in Mexico. To survive cold nights it can drop into torpor, slowing its heart and lowering its body temperature dramatically to conserve precious energy.
facts.Sandhill Crane: The sandhill crane is among the oldest surviving bird lineages, with fossil evidence stretching back millions of years, and it gathers in spectacular numbers, hundreds of thousands staging along Nebraska's Platte River each spring during migration. These tall grey cranes are famous for their elaborate dancing, bowing, leaping, and tossing vegetation, behavior used in courtship but performed by birds of all ages. They mate for life, and pairs perform synchronized 'unison calls' with trumpeting voices carried far by an elongated, coiled windpipe. Chicks, called colts, can follow their parents within hours of hatching.
facts.Satin Bowerbird: The satin bowerbird is one of nature's most fixated collectors, with mature males obsessively gathering blue objects, favoring flowers, feathers, berries, and human litter like bottle caps and drinking straws to adorn their twig avenues. Males take up to seven years to develop their glossy blue-black plumage and violet-blue eyes, spending their youth in green, female-like coloring. They even chew plant matter to make a bluish paint they smear on the bower walls. Females inspect dozens of bowers before choosing a mate, judging both decoration and dance.
facts.Scarlet Ibis: The scarlet ibis is famous for its almost unnatural brilliance, a deep red that comes entirely from carotenoid pigments in the crustaceans it eats. Chicks hatch dull grey and brown and acquire their full color only after years of a shrimp- and crab-rich diet. A wading bird of South American and Caribbean coasts, it probes soft mud with its long decurved bill to find prey by touch. It is the national bird of Trinidad and Tobago, where vast flocks roost together and turn the mangroves crimson at dusk.
facts.Scarlet Tanager: The breeding male Scarlet Tanager is brilliant red with jet-black wings and tail, but each autumn he molts into a patchy yellow-green plumage resembling the female before migrating to South America. Tanagers are canopy specialists, foraging high in deciduous forests for insects they often catch in flight or glean from leaves, and they will hawk bees and wasps, removing the stingers before eating. Their hoarse, burry song is sometimes likened to a robin with a sore throat. Long-distance migrants, they winter in the Andean foothills and Amazon basin before returning north to breed.
facts.Scissor-tailed Flycatcher: The scissor-tailed flycatcher's streaming forked tail can exceed its body length and snaps open and shut like shears during flight and courtship. A grassland specialist of the south-central United States and Mexico, it sallies from exposed perches like fence wires to hawk grasshoppers and other insects in midair. Males perform a dramatic 'sky dance,' climbing high then tumbling down in a series of zigzags and somersaults. Outside the breeding season, the birds gather in spectacular communal roosts that can number in the thousands.
facts.Secretarybird: The secretarybird is a long-legged bird of prey that stalks the African savanna on foot, a striking grey raptor with black 'plus-fours' on its thighs and a crown of quill-like crest feathers said to resemble a clerk's pens. It hunts by striking with astonishing force, stomping snakes and other prey with kicks delivered in milliseconds that land roughly five times its own body weight, accurate enough to crush a venomous serpent's skull before it can retaliate. It can fly well but covers vast ground walking, and pairs build broad stick platforms atop flat-topped acacias. It is now classified as endangered.
facts.Shoebill: The shoebill is a towering, prehistoric-looking wading bird of central African swamps, standing up to 1.4 metres tall with an enormous shoe-shaped bill edged with a sharp hook. It hunts with extraordinary patience, standing motionless for long stretches before lunging in a violent 'guillotine strike' to seize lungfish, often swallowing vegetation and decapitating prey in the process. Largely silent, it communicates by clattering its huge mandibles in rapid bursts that sound like machine-gun fire. It nests on floating platforms of vegetation and typically raises only a single chick to fledging.
facts.Snowy Owl: The Snowy Owl is among the heaviest North American owls, the females larger than the males and more heavily barred with dark flecks, while old males can fade to nearly pure white. Unlike most owls it is diurnal, hunting by day across open Arctic tundra where it relies almost entirely on lemmings, a single bird taking more than 1,600 in a year. Its breeding success tracks lemming population cycles so closely that in lean years pairs may not nest at all. In winters of high numbers, irruptions send these owls far south into fields, airports, and shorelines across the United States and Europe.
facts.Superb Fairywren: The Superb Fairywren is a tiny, long-tailed Australian songbird whose breeding males flush into brilliant iridescent blue and black. Despite living in tight family groups, they are among the most sexually unfaithful birds known, with most chicks in a nest fathered by males other than the social partner. Males court by carrying yellow flower petals and even perform displays in the predawn dark. Remarkably, females sing to their unhatched eggs, teaching a vocal password that the chicks must later reproduce to be fed, a defense against parasitic cuckoos.
facts.Superb Lyrebird: The male superb lyrebird is perhaps the most accomplished vocal mimic on Earth, weaving the calls of dozens of other species into his song along with mechanical sounds like camera shutters, chainsaws, and car alarms. During courtship he throws his enormous filamentary tail forward over his head into a shimmering silver canopy and dances on a cleared mound. Lyrebirds are ancient songbirds, and females also sing, often more complex songs than once believed. Despite their size they are shy ground-dwellers of southeastern Australian forests, scratching through leaf litter for invertebrates.
facts.Tawny Frogmouth: Despite its owl-like face, the tawny frogmouth is not an owl but a relative of the nightjars, hunting from a perch and taking insects, snails, and small vertebrates rather than seizing prey in flight. By day it roosts motionless on a branch, stretching its body stiff and upright with eyes narrowed so that it disappears into the limb as a broken stub of dead wood. Its mottled grey-brown plumage and wide, frog-like gape complete the disguise. Native to Australia, it is a nocturnal ambush hunter, often detected only by its low, repeated booming call after dark.
facts.Turkey Vulture: The Turkey Vulture possesses an extraordinary sense of smell, detecting the gases of decay from carrion more than a mile away, an ability so reliable that engineers once seeded natural-gas pipelines with the same scent and watched for circling birds to find leaks. It soars for hours on teetering, V-shaped wings, riding thermals with barely a flap. Lacking a strong voice box it can only hiss and grunt, and it cools itself by urinating on its own legs. Its featherless red head stays cleaner when plunged into rotting flesh, a tidy adaptation for a scavenger's diet.
facts.Vermilion Flycatcher: The male Vermilion Flycatcher is a blaze of brilliant red set against brown wings, and he courts females with a fluttering display flight, rising high while singing before parachuting slowly down. A classic sit-and-sally hunter, the bird perches on low exposed branches and darts out to seize flying insects before returning to the same spot. It ranges from the southwestern United States through Central and South America, favoring open country near water. Females and juveniles are far drabber, washed in soft peach and gray, making the male's color all the more striking.
facts.White-breasted Nuthatch: The White-breasted Nuthatch is famous for walking headfirst down tree trunks, a gravity-defying angle that lets it spot insects and spiders that upward-foraging birds overlook. It wedges large seeds and acorns into bark crevices and hammers them open with its bill, a behavior that gives the whole nuthatch family its name. To deter squirrels and predators it smears crushed insects around its nest hole, a chemical defense called bill-sweeping. Pairs hold their woodland territories all year and often join mixed winter foraging flocks with chickadees and titmice.
facts.Wilson's Bird-of-Paradise: Wilson's bird-of-paradise, found only on the Indonesian islands of Waigeo and Batanta, is among the smallest and most flamboyant of its family. The male's crown is bare turquoise skin so vivid it appears almost to glow, crossed by black lines, and his curled, wiry tail feathers spring out like twin violet hooks. Males meticulously clear and clean a small patch of forest floor as a display court, even stripping leaves overhead to let in light. Filmmaker David Attenborough's team captured the first quality footage of its display, lit from below by the cleared arena.
facts.Wood Duck: The Wood Duck is among the most ornately patterned of all waterfowl, the drake glowing with iridescent green, chestnut, and intricate white striping and a sweeping crest. It nests in tree cavities and readily takes to nest boxes, sometimes high above the ground. The day after hatching, the tiny ducklings climb to the cavity entrance and leap, dropping as much as fifty feet and bouncing unharmed off the leaf litter before toddling after their mother to water.
facts.Northern Goshawk: The Northern Goshawk is a powerful, secretive forest raptor with broad wings and a long rudder-like tail built for explosive bursts and tight maneuvering through dense timber. Adults wear slate-grey backs and a fierce red eye, and breeding birds are notoriously aggressive, striking intruders, including humans, who approach their nests. Across the boreal north their numbers rise and fall with cycles of snowshoe hares and grouse, and in lean winters they irrupt far south of their usual range in search of prey.
facts.Black Drongo: The Black Drongo is a glossy, fork-tailed songbird of open Asian farmland, jet-black with a startling red eye and a fearless temperament far exceeding its modest size. Known locally as the king crow, it boldly mobs crows, hawks, and even eagles, and other small birds often nest nearby to shelter under its aggressive protection. It hawks insects on the wing from exposed perches and is famous for mimicking other birds' calls, sometimes using false alarm calls to startle rivals off their food.
facts.Merlin: The Merlin is a small, compact falcon of open country and northern forests, a relentless aerial hunter that pursues songbirds in fast, low, powerful flight rather than the towering stoop of larger falcons. It rarely builds its own nest, instead commandeering the abandoned stick nests of crows and hawks. Once thinned by pesticides, Merlins have rebounded and increasingly adapted to towns and cities, where they hunt House Sparrows and feed on the abundant prey that urban edges provide.
facts.Steller's Jay: Steller's Jay is a bold, crested corvid of western pine and conifer forests, draped in deep charcoal and brilliant blue with a shaggy black topknot. A skilled mimic, it can imitate the scream of a Red-tailed Hawk to scatter other birds from a food source, then slip in to claim the spoils. Like other jays it caches thousands of seeds and nuts for winter, relying on sharp spatial memory, and it readily raids campsites and feeders with cunning opportunism.
facts.Hooded Merganser: The Hooded Merganser is North America's smallest merganser, a slender diving duck with a serrated bill perfectly shaped for gripping slippery fish and crayfish underwater. The breeding male raises a spectacular fan-shaped white crest bordered in black during his elaborate courtship displays. They nest in tree cavities, often near water, and the day after hatching the ducklings make a fearless leap from the high nest hole to follow their mother to the water below.
facts.Sanderling: The Sanderling is a small, plump sandpiper famous for its frantic dash along the surf line, sprinting after each retreating wave to snatch tiny crustaceans, then fleeing the next surge in a perpetual chase. Pale and almost ghostly in winter plumage, it breeds in the high Arctic tundra and winters on sandy beaches across nearly every continent, one of the world's most widely distributed shorebirds. Uniquely among sandpipers, it lacks a hind toe, an adaptation tied to its restless running.
facts.Hamerkop: The hamerkop, a stork relative from Africa and Madagascar, builds one of the largest nests of any bird, a massive domed fortress of sticks, mud, and grass that can exceed 1.5 meters across and bear the weight of a grown human. A breeding pair may construct several of these structures a year, each taking weeks and incorporating thousands of items, sometimes including odd debris like bones and plastic. Abandoned hamerkop nests become prized real estate for owls, geese, and even snakes. Its hammer-shaped head, formed by a backward crest, gives the bird its name.
facts.Mourning Dove: The mourning dove is among North America's most abundant and widely hunted birds, yet its population stays robust thanks to a prolific breeding habit, raising as many as six broods a season in warm climates. Its mournful, owl-like cooing is the song most people mistake for sorrow, and the sharp whistling of its wings on takeoff is produced by the feathers themselves, a built-in alarm. Pairs share incubation and feed their young a protein-rich 'crop milk' secreted by both parents. They swallow grit and seeds to store in the crop, digesting later from a safe perch.
facts.Eurasian Hoopoe: The Eurasian hoopoe is unmistakable, a cinnamon-pink bird with bold black-and-white wings and a fanning crest it raises like a startled headdress. It probes soil with its long curved bill for insect larvae and is famous for a pungent defense: nesting females and chicks secrete a foul, rotten-smelling oil from the preen gland, and the young can also blast intruders with feces. Its undulating, butterfly-like flight is distinctive across Europe, Asia, and Africa. The hoopoe appears in ancient Egyptian tomb art and is the national bird of Israel.
facts.Common Myna: The common myna, a bold and adaptable starling relative native to southern Asia, has become one of the world's most invasive birds, introduced across Australia, the Pacific, and beyond where it aggressively evicts native cavity-nesters. Highly intelligent and gregarious, mynas form lifelong pair bonds, gather in noisy communal roosts, and can mimic human speech in captivity. They thrive alongside people, foraging on insects, fruit, scraps, and roadkill. Their success has earned them a place among the IUCN's hundred worst invasive species.
facts.Common Tailorbird: The common tailorbird is a tiny warbler of South and Southeast Asian gardens that earns its name through extraordinary craftsmanship: it pierces the edges of one or more living leaves with its sharp bill and sews them together using plant fibre, spider silk, or even stolen thread, the punctures clenched into rivet-like knots. Inside this leaf cradle it builds a soft cup nest, hidden in plain sight. Despite its tailoring fame, it is more often heard than seen, delivering a loud, repetitive 'towit-towit' from dense cover. Both sexes share the stitching work.
